section_summary: This section contains U.S. Embassy Tokyo monthly reports on internal conditions in Japan and corresponding State Department Far Eastern Affairs analytical memoranda covering October 1932 through January 1933 (reporting on events from September through December 1932). It documents the diplomatic crisis surrounding the Lytton Report on Manchuria, Japan's defense at the League of Nations under Yosuke Matsuoka, and intense domestic budgetary clashes between military leaders and civilian officials over escalating expenditures. The files also detail the dampening of anti-American propaganda in Japan, emerging bilateral friction regarding American anti-dumping investigations, military action against General Su Ping-wen's rebellion in Manchuria, ultra-nationalist assassination plots, and banking consolidations under the 1927 Banking Law.

subfiles.about: Concluding section of Embassy Tokyo's monthly report for September 1932, covering emigration, anti-radical campaigns, distinguished visitors, and schedules of despatches and telegrams.
subfiles.summary: This concluding portion of Embassy Tokyo's September 1932 monthly report details Japanese emigration to São Paulo, Brazil, on the Rio de Janeiro Maru and ongoing police crackdowns against communist groups. It highlights notable arrivals and departures affecting Japanese-American relations, including aviator Wolfgang von Gronau, the return of the celebrated Japanese Olympic team, visits by Douglas Fairbanks and the University of Michigan baseball team, and a memorial service for Ransford S. Miller attended by Premier Makoto Saito. The document concludes with complete schedules of official despatches (Nos. 113 to 142) and telegrams (Nos. 223 to 246) transmitted by the Tokyo Embassy to the State Department during September 1932.
subfiles.title: Monthly Report on Conditions in Japan during the Month of September, 1932 (concluding section)

subfiles.about: Department of State Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizing Tokyo Despatch No. 174 enclosing the monthly report for October 1932.
subfiles.summary: The Division of Far Eastern Affairs summarizes Tokyo Despatch No. 174, highlighting conscious efforts by Japanese officials to restrain military-instigated anti-American sentiment, with Ambassador Katsuji Debuchi effectively silencing Foreign Office spokesman Toshio Shiratori. It analyzes Japanese reception of the Lytton Report and Japan's diplomatic strategy to delay proceedings before the League of Nations. The memorandum also reviews discussions regarding a Soviet-Japanese non-aggression pact, General Su Ping-wen's rebellion in Manchuria, secret Peruvian-Japanese arms-for-guano transactions, severe budgetary disputes between military and civilian officials, and planned emigration to the South Sea Mandated Islands and Brazil.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 174 (Monthly Report for October 1932)

subfiles.about: Embassy Tokyo's monthly report on Japanese political, diplomatic, military, financial, and economic conditions during October 1932.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 174 transmits Report No. 73 detailing Japanese affairs for October 1932, noting the subsidence of the military's anti-American propaganda campaign following September's spy scare, aided by Ambassador Debuchi's diplomacy and President Hoover's condolence message for lost Japanese aviators. The report assesses Japan's bitter reaction to the Lytton Commission findings, preparations for defense at Geneva by delegates Nagaoka, Sato, and Matsuoka, negotiations with Soviet officials, and the hostage crisis caused by General Su Ping-wen's revolt at Manchuli. Domestically, it covers huge budgetary demands by the Army and Navy under War Minister Araki, resistance from Finance Minister Takahashi, industrial export activity spurred by the depreciating yen, communist arrests, the territorial expansion of Greater Tokyo, and appended lists of October despatches and telegrams.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 174, Enclosing Report No. 73 on Conditions in Japan during the Month of October, 1932

subfiles.about: Department of State Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizing Tokyo Despatch No. 218 enclosing the monthly report for November 1932.
subfiles.summary: The Division of Far Eastern Affairs reviews Tokyo Despatch No. 218, noting the absence of active anti-American press agitation while warning that latent hostility persists. It discusses Japanese press sensitivity over American anti-dumping investigations, where the suspension of customs appraisements is viewed as an informal embargo. The memorandum outlines solid public backing for Yosuke Matsuoka at the League of Nations, military operations against General Su Ping-wen triggered by an intercepted telegram from T. V. Soong, the arrest of ultra-nationalist conspirators led by Hidezo Toyama plotting assassinations, and the newly established Manchukuo opium monopoly.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 218 (Monthly Report for November 1932)

subfiles.about: Embassy Tokyo's monthly report on conditions in Japan during November 1932, covering diplomacy at Geneva, domestic unrest, economic developments, and enclosed press editorials on U.S. dumping charges.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 218 transmits Report No. 74 on conditions in Japan for November 1932, noting the cessation of anti-American press attacks and public focus on Geneva, where Yosuke Matsuoka mounted a vigorous defense of Japanese policy before the League of Nations Assembly. The report details the Japanese military's suppression of General Su Ping-wen's revolt at Manchuli, the arrest of ultra-nationalist conspirator Hidezo Toyama and his gang for plotting the assassination of government and financial leaders, and sharp budget controversies between War Minister Araki and business leader Baron Goh. Appended materials include lists of despatches and telegrams, as well as enclosed editorials from The Japan Times and Osaka Asahi strongly protesting U.S. customs appraisal suspensions on Japanese tuna, salmon, and electric light bulbs.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 218, Enclosing Report No. 74 on Conditions in Japan during the Month of November, 1932, with Press Clippings

subfiles.about: Department of State Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizing Tokyo's monthly report on conditions in Japan for December 1932.
subfiles.summary: The Division of Far Eastern Affairs summarizes Tokyo's report for December 1932, observing quiet relations between Japan and the United States. It outlines internal political jockeying in the Diet, including Seiyukai maneuvers to unseat the cabinet and Kenzo Adachi's promotion of the new Kokumin Domei party. The memorandum highlights warnings from economists that Japan's export boom represents 'false prosperity' likely to worsen in late 1933, Finance Minister Takahashi's views on foreign exchange control, increases in commercial telegraph rates, and bank mergers under the 1927 Banking Law, which eliminated around 1,000 small banks.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Monthly Report for December 1932

subfiles.about: Transmittal despatch and opening sections of Embassy Tokyo's monthly report for December 1932, discussing Japanese-American relations and League of Nations proceedings.
subfiles.summary: This despatch transmits the Tokyo Embassy's report on Japanese conditions during December 1932, preceded by an Embassy summary sheet. It highlights stable Japanese-American relations, Japanese appreciation of American restraint toward the League of Nations, and proposed goodwill missions by Count Kabayama and Viscount Ishii. The report details the confrontation at the League of Nations Assembly, where Yosuke Matsuoka delivered an impassioned defense on December 6, vehemently opposed a censure resolution introduced by Czechoslovakia, Ireland, Sweden, and Spain, and threatened Japan's withdrawal from the League prior to the dispute's referral to the Committee of Nineteen.
subfiles.title: Despatch Enclosing Report on Conditions in Japan during the Month of December, 1932 (introductory section)
